Blifil also becomes a prospective husband for Sophia, less from affection than from the union of neighboring wealth. The private choices of Tom, Sophia, and Molly are increasingly constrained by families who treat marriage as property management.

Tom discovers that Molly has had other lovers and that he is not bound to marry her. He and Sophia acknowledge their love, but Squire Western's approval disappears when he understands that she prefers the penniless foundling to Blifil. Allworthy becomes dangerously ill. Tom's relief when his guardian recovers leads to drunken, disorderly behavior that Blifil presents as proof of ingratitude. By combining this incident with distorted accounts of Tom's earlier conduct, Blifil persuades Allworthy that Tom is corrupt. Allworthy banishes Tom and gives him money to begin elsewhere. Western tries to force Sophia to accept Blifil, so she leaves home with her maid Honour. Tom sets out without knowing that Sophia has also fled, and both are driven onto the road by the same marriage scheme.

Tom's journey becomes a succession of confused encounters in inns, military parties, and country houses. He briefly considers a military life and is injured in a quarrel. Benjamin Partridge, the schoolmaster once blamed for Tom's birth, reappears and attaches himself to Tom as companion and guide, hoping eventually to restore his own fortunes. Tom hears the long history of the solitary Man of the Hill, whose bitterness offers a warning against withdrawing from human society. Sophia and Honour travel separately, while Squire Western and others pursue them. Tom receives fragmentary signs that Sophia has passed nearby but repeatedly takes the wrong direction or is delayed by other people's crises. His generous impulses continue to help strangers, even as his impulsiveness makes reunion with Sophia less likely.

Near Upton, Tom rescues a woman calling herself Mrs Waters from an attack and brings her to an inn. Their intimacy there becomes another betrayal of the constancy he owes Sophia. Sophia reaches the same inn soon afterward and learns enough to believe Tom has immediately forgotten her. She leaves a personal token so he will know how closely he missed her, then continues toward London. A nighttime series of mistaken rooms, jealous spouses, and arriving pursuers throws the inn into disorder. Tom realizes Sophia is ahead of him and sets out after her, while Squire Western follows with the intention of taking his daughter home and forcing the marriage to Blifil. Mrs Fitzpatrick, fleeing her own unhappy marriage, becomes entangled with Sophia's journey and with the men searching for them.

Sophia reaches London and comes under the protection of her fashionable relative Lady Bellaston. Tom follows with Partridge and lodges in the generous Mrs Miller's household, where he befriends Mr Nightingale. Lady Bellaston desires Tom and offers him money and access; he becomes her secret lover partly in the hope of reaching Sophia. When Tom and Sophia finally meet, her love is mixed with anger at his repeated infidelity. Lady Bellaston works to keep them apart and to preserve her own control, while Tom tries to escape the affair without losing his path back to Sophia. His London life repeats the central conflict of his youth: real kindness and love coexist with appetites and rash choices that allow less generous people to control the appearance of events.

Tom uses a mock proposal of marriage to frighten Lady Bellaston into ending their affair, but the letter becomes further evidence against him when it reaches Sophia. Lady Bellaston promotes Lord Fellamar as Sophia's suitable husband. Fellamar attempts to force himself on Sophia, and her father's interruption saves her while also placing her back under family control. Western still insists on Blifil. Tom helps Nightingale accept responsibility and marry Mrs Miller's daughter Nancy, showing better judgment in his friend's case than in his own. After an encounter with the jealous Fitzpatrick, Tom wounds him in a duel and is sent to prison believing the man may die. Blifil and Lady Bellaston exploit Tom's danger, and Sophia has strong reason to think that his declarations of reform are only words.

Fitzpatrick survives, reducing the threat against Tom, while witnesses and long-concealed facts expose Blifil's campaign. Square leaves testimony correcting his earlier silence, and Allworthy learns that Tom's supposed ingratitude was repeatedly generosity misunderstood. Mrs Waters reveals that she is Jenny Jones and explains the secret of Tom's birth: Bridget Allworthy was his mother, and his father was a young man named Summer. Tom is therefore Allworthy's nephew. Blifil knew crucial parts of this history and suppressed evidence to secure the inheritance. Allworthy casts him out, though Tom asks that Blifil receive financial support. Sophia refuses to marry merely because Tom is now an heir and requires assurance that his behavior has changed. Convinced of his repentance, she forgives him. Tom and Sophia marry and build a happy family, while Allworthy recognizes Tom as both his relation and moral heir.

characters.description: An ordinary, mild-mannered Englishman whose morning begins with bulldozers arriving to demolish his house for a bypass. Bewildered and often still in his dressing gown, he is swept off the planet moments before its destruction and dragged through a series of cosmic events he barely understands. He spends much of his journey confused, indignant, and wishing for a decent cup of tea.
characters.name: Arthur Dent

characters.description: Arthur's friend of several years, who has passed as an out-of-work actor but is in fact an alien from a small planet near Betelgeuse and a roving researcher for the Guide. Stranded on Earth far longer than he intended, he keeps his composure in a crisis and rescues Arthur by hitching them both aboard a passing spaceship just before the planet is destroyed.
characters.name: Ford Prefect

characters.description: The captain of a Vogon Constructor Fleet, a bureaucratic and thoroughly unpleasant alien who oversees the demolition of Earth to clear the way for a hyperspace bypass. Devoted to paperwork and procedure and proud of his own extremely bad poetry, he inflicts a recital of it on the two stowaways he catches before having them thrown into space.
characters.name: Prostetnic Vogon Jeltz

characters.description: The flamboyant, self-obsessed former President of the Galaxy, who has two heads and three arms and a talent for outrageous stunts. Acting on impulses he does not fully understand himself, he steals a remarkable new starship, setting in motion the chase and the voyage that sweep up the others.
characters.name: Zaphod Beeblebrox

characters.description: A clever human woman with a background in mathematics and astrophysics, whom Arthur had once met and failed to impress at a party on Earth. She left the planet earlier in the company of Zaphod, and she now travels aboard his stolen ship, one of only a handful of humans left after Earth's destruction.
characters.name: Trillian

characters.description: A robot aboard the stolen starship, built with a vast intellect but afflicted by overwhelming boredom and depression. Convinced that his abilities are hopelessly wasted on trivial tasks, he complains constantly and views everything with gloom, though his gifts prove unexpectedly useful.
characters.name: Marvin

characters.description: An elderly designer of planets on the ancient world of Magrathea, who takes special pride in crafting elaborate coastlines. Kindly and a little wistful, he leads Arthur through a vast hidden factory and reveals the astonishing truth about what the planet Earth really was and why it was built.
characters.name: Slartibartfast

characters.description: A colossal supercomputer built long ago by a race of hyper-intelligent beings to determine the Answer to the ultimate question of Life, the Universe, and Everything. After calculating for millions of years, it delivers a result that its makers find both simple and useless without knowing what the actual question was.
characters.name: Deep Thought

characters.description: Hyper-intelligent, pan-dimensional beings who appear in our world in the humble form of laboratory mice. They are the ones who commissioned the building of the Earth for a grand experiment, and they take a keen and self-interested interest in what may have survived its destruction.
characters.name: The mice

recaps.ending: On Magrathea, Arthur discovers that the Earth was not simply a planet but an immense computer, built to work out the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything, to match the long-known Answer of 42. It was destroyed by the Vogons only minutes before it would have finished, after ten million years of running. The mice, hyper-intelligent beings who commissioned the whole experiment, decide that the last fragment of the program may be lodged in Arthur's brain and try to obtain it, first by offering to buy it and then by force. The attempt collapses when galactic police, chasing Zaphod for stealing the Heart of Gold, burst in shooting. Marvin, the depressed robot, plugs into the police ship's computer and makes it so miserable that it shuts itself down, killing the officers. Arthur, Ford, Zaphod, Trillian, and Marvin get away aboard the Heart of Gold. Hungry and shaken, they decide to go and eat at the Restaurant at the End of the Universe, leaving the question unresolved and their journey still under way.
recaps.in_short: Arthur Dent's house is about to be bulldozed when his friend Ford Prefect, secretly an alien, reveals that the whole Earth is about to be demolished by the Vogons to make room for a hyperspace bypass. Ford hitchhikes them onto a passing ship, and after being thrown out into space the pair are improbably rescued by the stolen starship Heart of Gold, crewed by Zaphod Beeblebrox, the two-headed former President of the Galaxy, the human Trillian, and the depressed robot Marvin. They travel to the myth-shrouded planet Magrathea, where Arthur learns that a supercomputer, Deep Thought, long ago found the Answer to Life, the Universe, and Everything to be 42, and that the Earth was an even greater computer, built to discover the actual question, destroyed just before it finished. The beings behind it, who appear as mice, want Arthur's brain. He escapes with the others, and they set off for the Restaurant at the End of the Universe.

recaps.text: Arthur Dent wakes to find bulldozers ready to knock down his house to build a bypass. His friend Ford Prefect, who is secretly an alien, tries to explain something far more urgent: the Earth itself is about to be destroyed. A fleet of Vogons arrives and demolishes the planet to clear a route for a galactic hyperspace bypass. Ford saves Arthur by hitchhiking them both aboard a Vogon ship in the last seconds before the end. Discovered as stowaways, the two are forced to endure a recital of dreadful Vogon poetry and are then thrown out into open space.

On the edge of death in the vacuum, Arthur and Ford are picked up, against staggering odds, by a stolen starship called the Heart of Gold, which runs on an Improbability Drive that makes wildly unlikely things happen. Aboard are the ship's thief, Zaphod Beeblebrox, the reckless two-headed former President of the Galaxy; Trillian, a human woman Arthur had once met at a party on Earth; and Marvin, a brilliant but hopelessly depressed robot. The unlikely group takes stock of one another as the ship carries them onward.

Zaphod steers the Heart of Gold toward Magrathea, a planet long dismissed as a myth, whose people once grew fabulously rich by building custom-made luxury worlds for the wealthy. As the ship approaches, automated defenses launch missiles at it. The crew survives when Arthur triggers the Improbability Drive, briefly turning the incoming missiles into harmless things, and they set down on the ancient, seemingly lifeless world to look for whatever remains of it.

On Magrathea, Arthur is led away by Slartibartfast, one of the old planet designers, who explains the world's history. Long ago a race of hyper-intelligent beings built a vast computer, Deep Thought, to find the Answer to the ultimate question of Life, the Universe, and Everything. After millions of years of calculation, Deep Thought delivered its result: the number 42, an answer that meant nothing to anyone, because no one actually knew what the ultimate question itself was.

To discover the question, Deep Thought designed an even greater computer to work it out: the planet Earth, with its living creatures and people forming part of a program meant to run for ten million years. The Vogons destroyed the Earth only minutes before the calculation would have finished. Arthur learns that the beings who commissioned the Earth appear in our world as mice, and that two of them were kept by Trillian as pets. Believing the last of the program may survive inside a human brain, they set out to obtain Arthur's.

Arthur refuses to give up his brain, and the mice's attempt to take it by force is interrupted when galactic police, hunting Zaphod for stealing the Heart of Gold, storm in and open fire. The confrontation ends when Marvin, connected to the police ship's computer, so thoroughly depresses it that it shuts itself down, killing the officers. Battered, hungry, and reunited, the group escapes together aboard the Heart of Gold and decides to travel on to the Restaurant at the End of the Universe, their adventures far from over.

characters.description: A comfortable, respectable hobbit of Bag End who wants nothing to do with adventures until Gandalf and a company of dwarves arrive uninvited and sweep him into a quest as their hired burglar. Fond of good food, his pipe, and his warm home, he surprises everyone - himself most of all - with unexpected nerve and cleverness once he is on the road east.
characters.name: Bilbo Baggins

characters.description: A wandering wizard famous for his fireworks and for a knack of drawing quiet folk into adventures. He arranges Bilbo's involvement with the dwarves and steers the company through its early dangers, though he comes and goes on errands of his own and does not stay with them the whole way.
characters.name: Gandalf

characters.description: The proud leader of the company of dwarves and heir to a kingdom beneath the Lonely Mountain that the dragon Smaug seized long ago. He means to reclaim his people's halls and treasure, and carries the weight of that lost inheritance with grave, sometimes stubborn, dignity.
characters.name: Thorin Oakenshield

characters.description: The wise and kindly master of Rivendell, the Last Homely House east of the mountains. He offers the travellers rest and reads the hidden moon-letters on their map, revealing a clue about the secret door into the Lonely Mountain.
characters.name: Elrond

characters.description: A slippery, secretive creature who lives on an island in a cold lake deep beneath the goblins' mountain, muttering to himself and hissing. He challenges the lost Bilbo to a riddle-game with high stakes, and guards a magic ring he calls his precious - a ring Bilbo happens upon in the dark tunnels.
characters.name: Gollum

characters.description: A huge, gruff man who can take the shape of a great bear, living alone with his remarkable animals in a hall between the mountains and Mirkwood. Wary of strangers, he nonetheless shelters and provisions the company once Gandalf carefully wins him over.
characters.name: Beorn

characters.description: The stern king of the wood-elves of Mirkwood, who holds the dwarves prisoner in his underground halls when they trespass in his forest. Fond of treasure and good wine, he is not evil but deeply suspicious of the travellers and their unexplained business.
characters.name: The Elvenking

characters.description: The great fire-breathing dragon who drove the dwarves from the Lonely Mountain generations ago and has slept on their heaped gold ever since. Cunning, vain, and immensely dangerous, he wakes when a thief disturbs his hoard and trades flattering, probing words with the unseen burglar who has crept into his lair.
characters.name: Smaug

characters.description: A grim, far-sighted man of Lake-town descended from the old lords of Dale, and a deadly archer. When the enraged dragon comes to burn the town, he alone keeps his head, and a whispered word about a bare patch in the beast's armor gives him his chance.
characters.name: Bard

recaps.ending: The book closes after the Battle of Five Armies. Thorin Oakenshield dies of his wounds, reconciled with Bilbo at the last, and his nephews Fili and Kili fall beside him; leadership of the mountain and its recovered wealth passes to Thorin's kinsman Dain. The alliance of dwarves, elves, and men that formed against the goblins holds afterward in friendship, the treasure is divided, and Bard rebuilds the ruined Lake-town and the old city of Dale. Bilbo, refusing all but a small share of the gold and silver, travels back to the Shire with Gandalf, resting again at Rivendell. He arrives to find he has been given up for dead and his home and belongings being auctioned off, and must reclaim them; his reputation among respectable hobbits never quite recovers, but he is content. He keeps the friendship of Gandalf and the surviving dwarves and settles back into a quiet life at Bag End. Crucially, he says nothing about the ring he found under the mountain, keeping it as a private curiosity. Neither he nor Gandalf yet understands what it truly is, a thread left hanging that will reopen years later when the ring's real nature and danger come to light.
recaps.in_short: Bilbo Baggins, a settled and unadventurous hobbit, is swept into an expedition with the wizard Gandalf and thirteen dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield to reclaim their ancestral treasure from the dragon Smaug. Along the way they survive trolls, goblins, and giant spiders; in the goblin-tunnels Bilbo finds a magic ring of invisibility, winning it from the creature Gollum after a riddle-game. He grows into a resourceful burglar, rescuing the dwarves from wood-elves by floating them downriver in barrels. At the Lonely Mountain he confronts Smaug and spots a weak point in the dragon's armor; Smaug then attacks Lake-town, where the archer Bard kills him. A quarrel over the treasure nearly sets dwarves, men, and elves against one another, but a goblin invasion forces them to unite in the Battle of Five Armies. Thorin dies reconciled with Bilbo, who returns home richer and wiser, quietly keeping the ring whose true nature no one yet suspects.

recaps.text: Bilbo Baggins, a comfortable and unadventurous hobbit of Bag End, is visited by the wizard Gandalf and then by thirteen dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield. Over supper Thorin explains their errand: long ago the dragon Smaug drove his people from the Lonely Mountain and seized their wealth, and the dwarves mean to reclaim it. Gandalf produces a map of the mountain and a key to a hidden side-door, and the reluctant dwarves accept Bilbo as their burglar. The company rides east. In the wild they are caught by three trolls who plan to eat them, but Gandalf keeps the trolls arguing until sunrise turns them to stone. From the trolls' hoard Gandalf and Thorin take two old elvish swords, and Bilbo picks up a small knife that will later serve him as a sword. They come to Rivendell, the valley of the elf-lord Elrond, who welcomes them and studies Thorin's map. By moonlight he reads hidden moon-letters on it, revealing that the secret door can only be opened at one time of year, when the last light of Durin's Day falls on the keyhole. Rested and better informed, the travellers press on toward the mountains.

Crossing the Misty Mountains, the company shelters in a cave that proves to be a goblin entrance; the goblins seize them and drag them underground. Gandalf reappears, kills the Great Goblin, and leads an escape, but in the dark Bilbo is knocked out and left behind. Groping along, he finds a plain gold ring lying on the stone and pockets it, then meets Gollum, a slimy creature dwelling by an underground lake. The two play a riddle-game with Bilbo's life as the stake, and Bilbo wins on a doubtful last question, asking aloud what he has in his pocket. Gollum paddles off to fetch his ring, finds it gone, and hunts Bilbo in a fury; Bilbo, slipping it on by chance, discovers it makes him invisible. He follows the raging Gollum to a back exit and escapes into daylight, rejoining the dwarves. Their relief is short-lived: wargs and goblins corner the company and drive them up trees, then set the trees alight. Great eagles, friends of Gandalf, swoop down and carry the whole party to safety.

The eagles set the travellers down near the home of Beorn, a fierce man who can take the shape of a great bear. Beorn feeds and re-equips them, then guides them to the edge of Mirkwood, a vast, dark, enchanted forest, where Gandalf leaves the company on other business. Warned to keep to the path, the dwarves and Bilbo push into the gloom. They nearly starve, Bombur falls into an enchanted stream and sleeps for days, and, straying off the track toward the lights of elvish feasts, they are trapped by giant spiders. Bilbo, using the ring and his little sword, which he now names Sting, kills several spiders and frees the dwarves. But wood-elves capture the company and imprison them in their king's caverns, holding Thorin separately. Bilbo, invisible, haunts the halls until he devises an escape: he packs the dwarves into empty wine barrels the elves are floating down the river and rides out clinging to a barrel himself. Bruised and soaked, they drift downriver toward Lake-town, in the shadow of the Lonely Mountain at last.

The barrels wash up at Lake-town, a settlement of Men built out over the Long Lake. The dwarves climb free and Thorin declares himself the King under the Mountain returned; the townsfolk, remembering old songs and hoping for renewed wealth, feast and outfit them, though the town's Master privately doubts the venture. After a time the company travels up to the Lonely Mountain and, guided by the map, searches its western side for the hidden door. They find the narrow ledge and the smooth stone but cannot open it, and days pass in frustration. At last, on the evening of Durin's Day, a thrush knocks a snail against the rock, the last ray of the setting sun strikes the wall, and a keyhole appears. Thorin fits his key, and the secret door swings inward, opening the dark passage that leads down toward the dragon's hall.

Bilbo is sent down the tunnel to face the dragon. Wearing the ring, he creeps into the treasure-hall and finds Smaug asleep on a mountain of gold. He steals a great cup, and later returns to trade riddling talk with the wakened dragon, flattering him into showing off his armored belly, and notices a bare patch on his left breast where the jeweled crust has not formed. A thrush overhears this. Smaug, certain the theft was aided by the men of Lake-town, flies off in the night to burn the town in revenge. Meanwhile the dwarves enter the hall, and Bilbo secretly finds and pockets the Arkenstone, the greatest jewel of Thorin's house. At Lake-town, Smaug rains fire on the roofs, but the archer Bard rallies the defenders. As the dragon wheels overhead, the thrush tells Bard of the bare patch; Bard looses his last black arrow into the gap, and Smaug crashes dead into the lake, wrecking the town as he falls. The homeless people look to Bard and turn their anger on the fleeing Master.

With the dragon dead, word of the unguarded hoard spreads. Bard, now hailed by the survivors, and the Elvenking of Mirkwood march to the mountain, Bard asking a share of the treasure as compensation for the ruin of Lake-town and for old wealth of his people. But Thorin, his mind poisoned by the gold, refuses every claim and sends word to his kinsman Dain to bring an army of dwarves from the Iron Hills. To break the deadlock and prevent bloodshed, Bilbo slips out at night and hands the Arkenstone to Bard and the Elvenking, giving them a bargaining piece Thorin cannot ignore. When Thorin learns of it he is enraged and names Bilbo a traitor. Just as dwarves, men, and elves stand ready to fight one another, a vast host of goblins and wolves pours out of the mountains, and the rival armies unite against them in the Battle of Five Armies. The fighting is desperate until the eagles and Beorn, in bear-shape, arrive; Beorn breaks the goblin ranks and the enemy is destroyed.

The victory is costly. Thorin is mortally wounded in the battle, and his nephews Fili and Kili die defending him. Before he dies, Thorin sends for Bilbo and makes peace with him, taking back his angry words and admitting the hobbit's worth. Dain becomes the new King under the Mountain, the treasure is fairly shared, and Bard rebuilds a town and rewards the survivors. Bilbo accepts only a modest chest or two of gold and silver, wanting no more. With Gandalf he journeys home the long way, resting again at Rivendell. Reaching the Shire, he finds himself presumed dead and his belongings up for auction; he has to buy back much of his own property and is regarded ever after as slightly disreputable for his adventuring. He settles again at Bag End, keeps up his friendships with the dwarves and Gandalf, and says nothing to his neighbours about the magic ring, which he quietly keeps.
